task: A centrally switched AP uses one untagged VLAN on its Ethernet link. Wireless client frames travel inside CAPWAP to the controller. Select the switchport mode; the access VLAN is configured separately.

teaching.hint: Follow the frames on this cable, not the wireless clients’ eventual VLANs.
teaching.takeaway: An access port is enough because only one untagged VLAN crosses this AP link. The clients’ VLANs appear at the controller, not at the AP.

task: This AP now switches client VLAN 20 locally with tags and sends management untagged in VLAN 10. The switch port is already a trunk with both VLANs allowed. Set its native VLAN to match the AP.

teaching.hint: The untagged management frames determine the native VLAN.
teaching.takeaway: The native VLAN carries the AP’s untagged management traffic; VLAN 20 stays tagged. The AP’s forwarding and tagging decide these settings, not the label “controller-based”.

task: An AP on SW1 FastEthernet0/1 has an Ethernet link but reports reduced radio operation. On a PoE-capable Cisco switch, display this port’s inline-power state and allocation.

teaching.hint: A link that is up does not show how much power the AP received.
teaching.takeaway: Compare the allocated power with the AP’s documented requirement and the switch’s remaining budget. An underpowered AP can join its controller and still limit its radios.

task: SW1 FastEthernet0/23 and 0/24 connect to an AireOS controller with LAG enabled. Both ports are already matching trunks. Add them to channel group 1 with the mode this controller requires.

teaching.hint: An AireOS LAG runs neither LACP nor PAgP.
teaching.takeaway: AireOS LAG is a static bundle, so the switch must also use static mode on. LACP active or PAgP desirable would wait for negotiation that the controller never sends.
